Slides (black), the doctor's notes (green), every gift (red) and the Aldughaither summary (grey, at the end).

Core approach — triple assessment

  • Triple assessment of a breast mass: H & PE → imaging (mammogram, US, MRI) → biopsy (core biopsy (TruCut), FNA).

Triple assessment: imaging and biopsy options

  • Any breast complaint or mass → triple assessment: (1) history + physical examination, (2) imaging, (3) biopsy/pathology when indicated. History and examination are always required; imaging and biopsy depend on age, complaint and suspicion.
  • Main breast complaints: lump, pain, nipple discharge, skin/nipple changes.
  • 47-year-old with a new 3-cm palpable mass → after history and examination: breast imaging followed by biopsy of the mass. 437 ×3

Breast imaging

ModalityBest forNotes (doctor)
MammographyMicrocalcifications, architectural distortion, screening, suspected malignancyBest in women ≥ 40 — fibroglandular tissue is replaced by fat with age → better penetration; less sensitive in dense young breasts
UltrasoundYoung/dense breasts; cyst vs solid; cysts, abscesses, fibroadenomaNot adequate alone for population screening, even in high-risk young women
MRIScreening selected very-high-risk patients; extent of known cancerUS may complement but does not replace MRI for high-risk screening
  • Breast mass in a woman ≥ 40 → mammogram + ultrasound.
  • Pregnancy: ultrasound first; if still suspicious, mammography with abdominal shielding is allowed; avoid contrast-enhanced MRI. Never postpone evaluation of a suspicious mass until after delivery.
  • 55-year-old with a 4 × 4 cm mass → investigation of choice mammogram 438 ×2; 50-year-old with bilateral upper-quadrant pain and tenderness → ultrasound + mammogram 438 ×4; a mammogram is ordered to look for microcalcifications. 438
  • 28-year-old with unilateral bloody discharge → ultrasound (young, dense breast). 438

Breast biopsy

MethodNotes
Core (true-cut) biopsyPreferred for a breast mass — keeps tissue architecture and the basement-membrane relationship → separates in situ from invasive disease
FNAIndividual cells only — not the right primary test when core biopsy is available; useful for a suspicious lymph node after cancer is diagnosed, and in other organs (thyroid)
  • Open incisional/excisional biopsy is not the routine first diagnostic step.

Differential diagnosis of a breast mass

  • Benign vs malignant.
  • Fibroadenoma · cyst · abscess · infection · lipoma · intraductal papilloma · juvenile fibroadenoma · phyllodes tumor · accessory breast tissue · fibrocystic changes.
  • Do not forget malignancy — even in young, pregnant or low-risk patients. Mastitis is usually diffuse, not a discrete mass, but can mimic one.
  • 19-year-old with a well-circumscribed, firm, smooth, mobile 3 × 4 cm lump → fibroadenoma. 442 ×6
  • Fibroadenoma management: 17-year-old, 4 cm, solid well-defined on US → clinical and radiological follow-up 442 ×2; 25-year-old, core-proven 4 cm → reassurance/follow-up or excision both accepted 437; 5 cm → excision (> 3–4 cm or growing → excise to exclude phyllodes) 435 ×2; fibroadenoma recall: options "> 5 cm / not capsulated" (a fibroadenoma is encapsulated and usually < 3 cm). 426
  • Painless irregular mass 5 months after trauma (car accident), true-cut biopsy → fat necrosis. 436

Fibrocystic changes

  • Previously "fibrocystic disease" — now part of the spectrum of benign/normal variation; nodularity/cysts that fluctuate with the cycle.
  • Cyclical pain worse before menses, lumpy nodular breasts with no discrete mass → fibrocystic changes 442 ×5; US shows multiple cysts of variable size. 431

Simple cyst

  • Aspirate if symptomatic/painful. Routine cytology of uncomplicated cyst fluid is not useful — suspected infection → culture; a suspicious lesion → imaging + tissue biopsy.
Doctor's notes: do not send simple cyst fluid for routine cytology. The past-exam key for the painful 4-cm simple cyst was "aspiration and send fluid for cytology" — follow the doctor in practice, but recognise the key. 437 ×2

Breast pain — mastalgia

  • Slides: describe the pain itself · cyclical vs non-cyclical · menarche vs 20s–30s vs elderly · with or without a mass.
  • Painful lump: fibroadenosis, cyst, periductal mastitis, abscess (usually postpartum/lactational), occasionally carcinoma. Pain and tenderness without a lump: cyclical pain, non-cyclical pain, very rarely carcinoma.
  • Pain history: unilateral/bilateral, cyclical/non-cyclical, breastfeeding, associated mass, onset, site/radiation, provoking/relieving factors, other breast/nipple/skin symptoms. Pain with a discrete mass has a different differential.
  • Painful breastfeeding: mastitis, abscess, nipple erosion, engorgement, galactocele (an infected galactocele can become an abscess).
  • Cancer can cause pain — don't dismiss malignancy because a lesion is painful.
  • Mastalgia = breast pain with no significant structural abnormality. Hormonal triggers: starting/stopping OCPs, fertility drugs, pregnancy, post-delivery. After imaging excludes pathology → reassurance is the main treatment (85–90% improve); analgesics, topical diclofenac, compresses, supportive bra, exercise, ↓ caffeine, stress management, low-fat diet, evening primrose oil/vitamin E; rare refractory cases → tamoxifen.

Infection — mastitis & abscess

  • Breast abscess → ultrasound-guided needle aspiration (may need repeating); avoid formal I&D when aspiration works (less scarring). Antibiotics, especially if drainage is incomplete.
  • Refractory/recurrent abscess → think: inadequate drainage, wrong antibiotic, resistant organism, underlying malignancy; send aspirate for culture.
  • Galactocele: milk-filled collection in lactation; reassurance if asymptomatic, aspiration if painful; can become infected.
  • Lactating woman, breast pain + fever for one day, normal US → mastitis 439 ×4; erythematous tender, not fluctuant, normal US → continue breastfeeding + antibiotics. 442
  • Lactational mastitis/periareolar infection → flucloxacillin (S. aureus) 435 ×5 427 ×2
  • "Cellulitis" recurring 5 times despite antibiotics → skin biopsy (exclude inflammatory breast cancer). 441
  • Inflammatory breast cancer may mimic mastitis/abscess (erythema, swelling, peau d'orange, rapid progression, "refractory infection") — if infection doesn't settle with drainage + antibiotics, biopsy.

Nipple changes & discharge

Displacement and deviation · retraction and displacement by an underlying carcinoma

Retraction with peau d'orange · destruction of the nipple by carcinoma

Duct ectasia (transverse slit nipple) · mammillary duct fistula after periductal mastitis

Paget's disease of the nipple · eczema vs Paget's disease

  • New retraction, destruction or deviation → malignancy until proven otherwise. Key question: is it new or the patient's baseline?
  • Duct ectasia: dilated ducts, usually older women, often asymptomatic; secretions → discharge, retraction-like nipple, occasional inflammation/abscess. Benign — no treatment if asymptomatic once cancer is excluded.
  • 47-year-old with nipple retraction, multiple-duct discharge, no mass, dilated ducts on US → duct ectasia 438 ×3; its discharge is mixed/multicoloured (green, white, brown) 439 439 ×2
  • Paget disease: malignant change of nipple/areolar skin, ± underlying carcinoma, may have no mass; older woman, unilateral, progressive, nipple erosion, less itchy than eczema → skin biopsy + imaging; treated as breast cancer (central excision removing the NAC, ± systemic/RT).

Nipple discharge

  • Slides: colour · character · time · spontaneous or not · with a mass · with nipple change · could it be physiological?

Decoding nipple discharge by colour · physiologic vs pathologic discharge

  • History: colour, spontaneous vs expressed, unilateral/bilateral, mass, skin changes, age/menopause, pregnancy/lactation, drugs/endocrine.
ColourSignificance (doctor)
Bloody / serous / clearMost concerning — especially spontaneous, unilateral, with a mass or nipple change, or in a postmenopausal woman
Green / brownGenerally reassuring — fibrocystic/ductal benign changes
MilkyLactation, prolactinoma/hyperprolactinaemia, drugs, other hormonal causes
  • Bloody discharge — most common benign cause: intraductal papilloma (cancer still excluded by triple assessment). Excise if atypia, persistent symptomatic bleeding or concerning lesion; papilloma without atypia may be observed.
  • 28-year-old, bloody discharge, no mass, normal US → intraductal papilloma. 441 ×6
  • Headache, visual change and bilateral milky discharge → serum prolactin (and TSH) (pituitary prolactinoma). 441

History points & red flags

  • Lump & nodularity: like any lump — history and examination; a lump vs enlargement of the whole breast; relation to hormonal status and breastfeeding; family history; other lumps (axilla).

Breast lumps and skin contour changes

Massive breast enlargement · ulcerating fungating tumour

A simplified plan for diagnosing common breast lumps · comparison of the four common lumps (cyst, nodularity, fibroadenoma, carcinoma)

  • Skin changes & ulceration:

Peau d'orange — compare the skin of an orange

Skin nodules/inflammation over a large tumour · skin ulceration

  • Mass history: duration, change in size, pain, mobility, cyclical variation, pregnancy/breastfeeding, menopausal status, hormone therapy, discharge, skin change, family history (which relative, how many, age at diagnosis), previous radiation.
  • Mantle-field radiation for lymphoma at a young age → markedly ↑ breast-cancer risk ~10+ years later → high-risk screening.
  • Skin tethering/dimpling (tumor fibrosis of suspensory ligaments); peau d'orange (dermal lymphatic obstruction — also severe infection); ulceration/fungating lesion → advanced malignancy until proven otherwise.

Phyllodes tumor & large masses

  • Juvenile fibroadenoma: adolescents, can become very large — size alone ≠ malignancy.
  • Phyllodes: fibroepithelial, more cellular than fibroadenoma; benign / borderline / malignant; rapid growth → huge mass, skin ischaemia/ulceration. Malignant phyllodes behaves like a sarcoma → haematogenous spread (lymphatic uncommon).
  • Core biopsy may not separate it from fibroadenoma. Treatment: excision with a ≈ 1-cm clear margin for all categories.
  • Phyllodes (4.5 cm) → wide local excision with ≥ 1 cm margin — no sentinel node (rarely spreads to nodes). 442 439

Other

  • Breast enlargement: bilateral or unilateral; physiological (e.g. pregnancy, puberty); gynaecomastia.

Gynaecomastia

  • Accessory breast tissue (axilla) and supernumerary nipple (along the milk line) — benign; excise for cosmetic/symptomatic reasons.
  • Nodularity ≠ mass — young breasts feel nodular, especially upper outer quadrant/axillary tail.
  • Gynecomastia = benign enlargement of male glandular tissue (oestrogen effect): puberty (often unilateral/asymmetric), older age, obesity, drugs, anabolic steroids, liver cirrhosis, alcoholism, hormone-producing tumors.
  • Male breast cancer: a new unilateral mass or unilateral gynecomastia in an adult man is concerning until proven otherwise.
  • 10-year-old boy with gynecomastia, no mass, normal US → observe and follow up. 439
  • Upper-limb lymphedema after breast-cancer surgery comes from axillary lymphatic disruption — sentinel node biopsy limits it.

Breast Disorders (Excluding Cancer)

Benign Breast Disorders: Fibrocystic Condition
Overview
  • Common benign breast condition affecting 30-50 years age group.
  • Rare in postmenopausal women not on hormone replacement therapy.
  • Hormonal influence: Estrogen is a significant factor.
  • Characterized by multiple, often bilateral cystic breast masses.
Clinical Presentation
Symptoms
  • Breast masses: Often multiple and bilateral.
  • Pain & tenderness:
  • Worsens before menstruation (cyclical).
  • Improves after menstruation.
  • Fluctuating mass size:
  • Rapid appearance/disappearance of lumps.
  • Masses shrink post-menses.
  • Serous nipple discharge (clear or slightly yellow).
Physical Examination
  • Rubbery, mobile breast lumps.
  • Diffuse nodularity with no distinct dominant mass.
  • Tenderness on palpation.
Diagnosis
1. Imaging
  • Mammography: Recommended for women ≥30 years.
  • Ultrasound:
  • Preferred in women <30 years (denser breast tissue).
  • Differentiates solid vs. cystic masses.
2. Biopsy
  • Core needle biopsy (preferred over FNA).
  • Fine-needle aspiration (FNA):
  • Can confirm the cystic nature of the lump.
  • Not recommended for suspicious masses.
  • Excisional biopsy:
  • Reserved for discordant imaging & biopsy results.
Differential Diagnosis
  • Breast carcinoma:
  • Fixed, non-mobile, irregular, firm mass.
  • No cyclic size variation.
  • Fibroadenoma:
  • Mobile, rubbery, well-circumscribed.
  • Common in young women.
  • Intraductal papilloma:
  • Bloody nipple discharge.
Treatment & Management
1. Conservative Management
  • Supportive bra: Reduces discomfort.
  • Avoid trauma: Can worsen symptoms.
  • Pain relief:
  • NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen, topical diclofenac).
  • Evening primrose oil (γ-linolenic acid): Reduces pain in 44%-58% of women.
  • Vitamin E (400 IU daily): Anecdotal benefit.
2. Hormonal Therapy (for severe pain)
  • Danazol (100-200 mg BID): FDA-approved but rarely used due to androgenic side effects.
  • Tamoxifen: Reduces symptoms but not recommended for young women.
  • Modify HRT (postmenopausal women): Reducing estrogen dose may alleviate pain.
3. Dietary & Lifestyle Modifications
  • Caffeine restriction (controversial).
  • Low-fat diet: May improve symptoms.
4. Aspiration
  • Indicated for painful, fluid-filled cysts.
  • Follow-up: If the cyst recurs or contains bloody fluid, a biopsy is necessary.
Prognosis & Cancer Risk
  • Symptoms improve after menopause unless on HRT.
  • Increased breast cancer risk in:
  • Atypical epithelial hyperplasia.
  • Papillomatosis.
  • Increased mammographic density.
  • Regular self-exams & clinical follow-ups are essential.
Fibroadenoma of the Breast
Overview
  • Most common benign breast tumor in young women (usually within 20 years after puberty).
  • More frequent and occurs earlier in Black women.
  • Multiple fibroadenomas are seen in 10%-15% of patients.
  • Rarely occurs after menopause, unless hormone therapy is used.
Clinical Features
  • Firm, rubbery, round/ovoid, well-circumscribed, mobile, and non-tender mass.
  • Size: Typically, 1-5 cm in diameter.
  • No cyclic variation in size (unlike fibrocystic condition).
  • Often discovered incidentally.
  • Does not cause nipple discharge or skin changes.
  • Larger fibroadenomas (>3-4 cm) require evaluation to rule out phyllodes tumors.
Diagnosis
1. Clinical Examination
  • Well-defined, freely mobile breast lump ("breast mouse").
  • Usually non-tender.
  • No skin changes.
2. Imaging
  • Ultrasound (first-line in women <30 years):
  • Well-defined, oval mass with smooth margins.
  • Homogeneous hypoechoic lesion.
  • "Popcorn calcification" (seen in older fibroadenomas).
  • Mammography (used in women >30 years):
  • Well-circumscribed, oval/round, dense mass.
  • May have coarse calcifications.
3. Biopsy
  • Core needle biopsy (preferred):
  • Confirms diagnosis.
  • Fine-needle aspiration (FNA):
  • Used in some cases but less accurate.
  • Excisional biopsy:
  • Indicated if the lesion is ≥3-4 cm, growing, or uncertain in diagnosis.
Differential Diagnosis
ConditionKey Features
Fibrocystic ChangesCyclical pain, multiple lumps, fluctuating size.
Breast CystWell-defined, fluid-filled, resolves after aspiration.
Phyllodes TumorRapidly growing, can be benign or malignant.
Breast CancerHard, fixed, irregular mass, skin changes, nipple retraction.
Management
1. Conservative Management
  • If the diagnosis is confirmed by core biopsy & no symptoms → No treatment is required.
  • Regular follow-up with breast exams and ultrasound.
2. Surgical Options
  • Excision (if any of the following are present):
  • >3-4 cm in size (rule out phyllodes tumor).
  • Rapid growth.
  • Uncertain diagnosis.
  • Cryoablation:
  • Freezing the fibroadenoma.
  • Used for biopsy-confirmed fibroadenomas.
  • May leave a scar or fat necrosis, with no clear advantage over observation.
Phyllodes Tumor vs. Fibroadenoma
FeatureFibroadenomaPhyllodes Tumor
GrowthSlowRapid
SizeUsually <3 cmOften >3-4 cm
HistologyFibroepithelial tumorMore cellular stroma
RiskBenignCan be benign or malignant
TreatmentExcision if largeWide local excision (to prevent recurrence)
  • Malignant phyllode tumors may require total mastectomy, but lymph node dissection is NOT needed.
Prognosis
  • Fibroadenomas do not increase breast cancer risk.
  • Recurrence is rare after excision.
  • Phyllodes tumors may recur locally if not adequately excised.
Nipple Discharge
Overview
  • Most common causes in non-lactating women: 1. Duct ectasia 2. Intraductal papilloma 3. Carcinoma (less common but important to rule out)
  • Evaluation of discharge characteristics is essential to differentiate benign from malignant causes.
Types of Nipple Discharge & Their Causes

Clinical Evaluation
1. History & Physical Examination
  • Key questions:
  • Unilateral or bilateral? → Unilateral raises concern for malignancy.
  • Spontaneous or provoked? → Spontaneous is more concerning.
  • Single or multiple ducts? → Single-duct is more suspicious for carcinoma.
  • Color and consistency of discharge?
  • Presence of associated breast mass?
  • History of recent pregnancy, medications, or hormonal therapy?
  • Menstrual cycle relation?
  • Symptoms of systemic disease (e.g., headaches, visual changes for pituitary tumor)?
2. Diagnostic Workup
  • Mammography & Ultrasound:
  • Indicated for women >30 years or palpable mass.
  • Can identify papillomas, ductal dilatation, or malignancies.
  • Ductography (Galactography):
  • Mammogram with contrast injected into the duct.
  • Used for single-duct, spontaneous discharge.
  • Cytology of Nipple Discharge:
  • Limited value, as negative cytology does not rule out cancer.
  • Serum Prolactin & TSH:
  • Indicated for milky discharge to rule out hyperprolactinemia or hypothyroidism.
  • MRI:
  • Used in high-risk patients or indeterminate imaging findings.

Discharge
When to Suspect Cancer
High suspicion for malignancy if:
  • Unilateral
  • Spontaneous discharge
  • Bloody or serosanguineous discharge
  • Associated mass
  • Age >50 years
→ Requires duct excision for diagnosis and treatment!
Fat Necrosis of the Breast
Overview
  • Rare benign breast lesion.
  • Can mimic carcinoma clinically and radiologically.
  • Causes:
  • Trauma (blunt injury, surgery, seat belt injuries).
  • Fat grafting procedures (breast augmentation, post-surgical defect filling).
  • Radiation therapy.
  • Breast reconstruction (flap procedures after mastectomy).
  • Post-segmental resection (lumpectomy).
Clinical Features
Symptoms
  • Firm, irregular mass that may feel hard and fixed.
  • Painless or tender (depends on inflammation).
  • Skin or nipple retraction (can resemble malignancy).
  • May have localized bruising or redness initially.
  • No axillary lymphadenopathy.
Physical Examination
  • Ill-defined, non-mobile mass.
  • Possible overlying skin changes (thickening, dimpling).
  • No rapid progression (unlike carcinoma).
Diagnosis
1. Imaging Studies
  • Mammography:
  • Oil cysts, calcifications, or spiculated masses (can mimic cancer).
  • Ultrasound:
  • Hypoechoic mass, cystic changes, or shadowing.
  • MRI:
  • Fat-containing lesion with a rim of enhancement.
  • Helps differentiate from malignancy.
2. Biopsy
  • Core needle biopsy (preferred):
  • Confirms necrotic fat cells, foamy macrophages, and fibrosis.
  • Excisional biopsy:
  • Done if imaging and core biopsy are inconclusive.
Management
1. Conservative Management
  • If diagnosis is confirmed and no symptoms → Observation.
  • Most cases resolve spontaneously.
  • NSAIDs for pain relief.
2. Surgical Excision
  • Indications:
  • Persistent mass or worsening symptoms.
  • Imaging is not typical for fat necrosis.
  • Concern for malignancy.
Breast Abscess
Overview
  • Localized breast infection with pus collection.
  • Most common in lactating women (lactational mastitis progressing to abscess).
  • Staphylococcus aureus is the most frequent pathogen.
  • Non-lactational abscesses are rare but may be associated with chronic infections, smoking, diabetes, or malignancy.
Types of Breast Abscesses
1. Lactational (Puerperal) Abscess:
  • Occurs during breastfeeding due to milk stasis.
  • Painful, swollen, red mass.
  • Commonly in the upper outer quadrant.
  • S. aureus is the most common causative organism.

2. Non-Lactational Abscess:

  • Occurs in non-breastfeeding women.
  • Subareolar abscess is common in smokers (periductal mastitis).
  • May be linked to diabetes, steroid use, nipple piercings, hidradenitis suppurativa, or inflammatory carcinoma.
Clinical Features
Symptoms
  • Painful, warm, erythematous mass.
  • Fever, chills, and malaise (suggests systemic infection).
  • Fluctuant mass on examination.
  • Purulent nipple discharge (sometimes).
  • Axillary lymphadenopathy (in severe infections).
Physical Examination
  • Tender, indurated, erythematous area.
  • Fluctuance suggests pus collection.
  • Non-lactating abscesses may be associated with nipple retraction or duct ectasia.
Diagnosis
1. Clinical Diagnosis
  • Based on physical examination in lactating women.
2. Imaging Studies
  • Ultrasound:
  • Identifies fluid collection.
  • Differentiates mastitis from an abscess.
  • Mammography (for non-lactating women):
  • Rules out malignancy (especially if recurrent abscess or abnormal skin changes).
3. Laboratory Tests
  • Culture and Sensitivity:
  • If aspiration or drainage is performed.
  • Helps tailor antibiotic therapy.
Management
1. Antibiotic Therapy
  • Empiric antibiotics covering Staphylococcus aureus:
  • Dicloxacillin or cephalexin (for mild cases, no MRSA suspicion).
  • Clindamycin or Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) (if MRSA suspected).
  • Vancomycin (IV) for severe cases.
  • Duration: 10–14 days.
  • Continue breastfeeding if possible.
2. Drainage Procedures
  • Needle Aspiration (First-line for Small Abscesses):
  • Ultrasound-guided aspiration.
  • Less invasive and preserves cosmetic appearance.
  • Incision and Drainage (I&D) (for Larger or Recurrent Abscesses):
  • Done if aspiration is ineffective.
  • Excision of the infected lactiferous ducts may be necessary for recurrent subareolar abscesses.
3. Supportive Care
  • Warm compresses to reduce pain and swelling.
  • Analgesics (e.g., ibuprofen, acetaminophen).
  • Frequent breastfeeding or pumping to prevent milk stasis.
Special Considerations
  • Inflammatory Breast Cancer:
  • If an abscess does not resolve with antibiotics, biopsy to rule out malignancy.
  • Signs to watch for:
    • Persistent erythema, peau d'orange, or skin thickening.
    • Nipple retraction or bloody discharge.
Prognosis
  • Good response to antibiotics and drainage.
  • Recurrence is rare if treated appropriately.
  • Chronic or recurrent abscesses require further evaluation for malignancy or ductal involvement.
